explanation: Fires on a highly predictable next word inside a stock or boilerplate phrase. The strongest cases are software-license boilerplate ('retain the above copyright [notice]', 'Apache [License]', 'Google [Inc]', 'non[exclusive]') and fixed expressions like 'round to the [nearest]', 'one for [every]', 'dozens and [dozens]', 'out [of] the ordinary'. Tokens in ordinary free prose give little or nothing.

Fires on a determiner ('the', 'a', 'an', 'this') that opens the object noun phrase right after a verb or preposition, as in legal 'appeals from [a] decree', 'Apple Inc. and [the] Swift', '([the] "License")', 'increase [the] ...'. Separately it fires on the PHP '$' sigil after '=' or at the start of a statement ('$result = [$]search').

No clear shared feature. It fires on assorted tokens: 'and' joining two verb phrases in how-to questions, prepositions like 'in'/'on' after a noun in descriptions, pieces of proper names (Silesian, Deportivo, Dailymotion), dict keys in code, and '::' in Ruby.

A mixture. Strongest: 'from' in court-caption 'Appeal from the United States District Court', '.m' in Objective-C file-header comments, 'COM' in the AssemblyInfo comment, and scattered tokens inside boilerplate (Boost/GPL license addresses, C# '{ get; set; }').

Fires on a word-internal subword fragment (usually the first or second piece) of a word split into several tokens. It is strongest in non-English text (German, Portuguese, French, Romanian), e.g. 'vor[ang]egangenen', '[restr]ito', 'celăl[alt]', and also on rarer English words (pan|icking, herm|aph, f|oment). Whole common words give little.

Fires on the first token inside an opening parenthesis in prose, especially '(and', '(or', '(by', '(only', '(yet', '(the'. The token right after '(' gets the high activation. The '(' itself before an acronym, or a parenthesis in math or code, gives only weak to moderate activation.

A mixture. It fires on the '.\n' ending a paper-title line before the abstract body, on tokens after 'type' or '@' in JS/JSDoc ('type[:] Array', '*[ @]param'), on '(at' in the GPL clause, and on function words like 'to' or 'a' following a verb in expository prose.

Fires on 'AM'/'PM'/'am'/'pm' right after a clock time (e.g. '9:06 [AM]', '10:26[pm]'), in email headers, timestamps and post dates. Weaker offshoot: short capital-letter or fragment pieces inside abbreviations or names (MOT[U], MS[U], [MT]I, Makefile[.am]).

Fires on a digit token in the middle of a multi-digit number, typically the second digit right after the leading one (2[2]9, -3[0]6, 4[1]:660, 5,[2]10). It covers citations, populations, patent numbers and sequences, including full-width digits. Lone single-digit numbers and the first digit fire little.

Fires on the stem fragment of a verb split into several subword tokens, mainly German/Dutch verbs (sp[ü]ren, re[chn]en, [erk]ennen, ver[urs]achen) and Latinate English verbs (re[oc]cur, [reminis]ce, [exacerb]ate, [substant]iate). Whole-word verbs and non-verbs fire weakly.

Fires on words expressing hope, aim or a helpful positive outcome in a friendly service or advice voice. 'hopefully' fires strongest, then 'hope', 'cope', 'work hard [to]', 'make you [feel]', 'make the [most]'. There is a minor offshoot on '#ifndef' after a Boost license header.

Fires on a bare-infinitive action verb right after 'to', 'how to', 'can't'/'can not' or a similar complement, e.g. 'How to [access]', 'methods to [monitor]', 'reorgan[ize]', 'can't [escape]'. Copulas and auxiliaries ('be', 'were', 'are') fire weakly.

Fires on capitalized word-initial fragments 'Qu'/'McGu'/'Cl'/'Gu' that begin a name or word split into subwords (McGu|ire, Qu|ercus, Qu|etta, Cl|arence), including lowercase 'qu' in Romance languages. Other tokens give at most weak activation.

Two unrelated patterns. One is the negative prefixes 'un'/'non' at the start of a split word (un|loading, un|skilled, non-functioning). The other is prepositions or numerals in travel, aviation and price contexts ('travelling [on] leave', 'fly on [a] commercial airline', 'overflight [of]', 'tariffs [on]'). There are also some non-Latin-script fragments.

Strongest on light verbs in idiomatic verb-object phrases, especially 'take'/'took'/'taking' (part, payments, applicants' race into) and 'go'/'goes' (on, beyond), and also 'pay' (the bills). It also fires scattered on prepositions ('formation [of]', 'dismissed for 5 runs [by]') and pieces of names, so the picture is mixed.

A mixture. It fires on count words before a sports statistic ('contributing with [two] goals', 'recorded [one] goal', 'his [second]', 'thrown [an] NFL pass') and on '=' in definitions or assignments ('GA [=]', '$input [=]'). It also fires on verbs or prepositions in methods text ('entered [into]', '[used] Cox').

Fires on a middle or final subword piece of a rare proper name or technical term that is split into several tokens: personal and place names (Al-Sah[li], Kam[al], Dü[za]ğaç), chemical and drug names (Methylglyox[al], isoproteren[ol]), and taxonomic names (I[lex]). Common words fire little.

In code, fires on the array or collection name or the '[' token just before an index subscript ('str[[]0]', 'names[i]', 'split(',')[0]', 'hsvChannels[0]'). It also fires on nearby pointer or type tokens in loops over arrays. Prose fires essentially not at all.

No coherent pattern. It fires on medical-term fragments (al[ve]olar, a[ort]omesenteric, cardio[verter]), modal or legal words ('shall', 'either', 'could'), Q&A markers ('A', 'Let'), and fragments of non-English words.

Mostly fires on a preposition or function word inside a multiword name or fixed phrase ('University [of]', 'University [in] St. Louis', 'Schools [of] Excellence', 'División [de]', 'stock [in]', 'removed [from]'). It also has scattered unrelated hits in code and SVG paths, so it is mixed.
